greek: Habentes itaque regulam ipsam veritatem, et in aperto positum de Deo testimonium, non debemus per quaestionum declinantes in alias atque alias absolutiones ejicere firmam et veram de Deo scientiam: magis autem, absolutionem quaestionum in hunc characterem dirigentes, exerceri quidem convenit per inquisitionem mysterii et dispositionis existentis Dei, augeri autem in caritate ejus, qui tanta propter nos fecit et facit, nunquam autem excidere ab ea suasione qua manifestissime praedicatur, quia hic solus vere sit Deus et Pater, qui et hunc mundum fecit, et hominem plasmavit, et in sua creatura donavit incrementum.
greek_edition: Latin: Harvey, W. W. (ed.), Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, Cambridge 1857 (scan vol. 1: archive.org sanctiirenaeiep01harvgoog), read from archive.org djvu OCR (https://archive.org/details/sanctiirenaeiep01harvgoog); ligatures normalised (ae/oe). OCR prints 'Hasenres' for 'Habentes'. Not visually checked on the scan. No Greek survives for this sentence.
english: Having therefore the truth itself as our rule and the testimony concerning God set clearly before us, we ought not, by running after numerous and diverse answers to questions, to cast away the firm and true knowledge of God. But it is much more suitable that we ... should exercise ourselves in the investigation of the mystery and administration of the living God, and should increase in the love of Him who has done, and still does, so great things for us; but never should fall from the belief by which it is most clearly proclaimed that this Being alone is truly God and Father ... (ANF 2.28.1, Roberts & Rambaut, abridged with ellipses).
page: printed p.349 (Harvey vol. 1); ANF page unknown
edition: Harvey 1857 (Cambridge), scan vol. 1; ANF vol. 1 (1885) for English
what_it_says: Irenaeus tells the reader to keep the firm knowledge of God and not chase answers; the dispositio of God is said to be a matter of inquiry to be exercised within faith.
limits: Sentence 'quia hic solus vere sit Deus et Pater' (this One alone is truly God and Father) is itself quoted by unitarians; it is directed at the Demiurge debate. Dispositionis (ANF 'administration') has no surviving Greek here. OCR only for p.349.

greek: Scripture[ae] quidem perfectae sunt, quippe a Verbo Dei et Spiritu ejus dictae; nos autem secundum quod minores sumus et novissimi a Verbo Dei et Spiritu ejus, secundum hoc et scientia mysteriorum ejus indigemus.
greek_edition: Latin: Harvey, W. W. (ed.), Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, Cambridge 1857 (scan vol. 1: archive.org sanctiirenaeiep01harvgoog), read from archive.org djvu OCR (https://archive.org/details/sanctiirenaeiep01harvgoog); ligatures normalised (ae/oe). OCR prints 'Scripture' for 'Scripturae' (bracketed ae is an assumption). Harvey's English footnote 1 on p.349 comments that the phrase expresses 'the doctrine of the Trinity'; that is the editor's gloss, not Irenaeus.
english: ...the Scriptures are indeed perfect, since they were spoken by the Word of God and His Spirit; but we, inasmuch as we are inferior to, and later in existence than, the Word of God and His Spirit, are on that very account destitute of the knowledge of His mysteries. (ANF 2.28.2)
page: printed pp.349-350 (Harvey vol. 1); ANF page unknown
edition: Harvey 1857 (Cambridge), scan vol. 1; ANF vol. 1 (1885) for English
what_it_says: Scripture is spoken by the Word of God and His Spirit together, and humans are later than both.
limits: Says Word and Spirit together dictated Scripture and are prior to creatures ('later in existence'); does not say they are consubstantial or eternal in so many words. The Trinitarian reading is Harvey's footnote, not the Latin. OCR only for p.349-350.

greek: Oportet enim eum prae omnibus praecellere. Quid enim si tentemus exponere causam ascensionis Nili?
greek_edition: Latin: Harvey, W. W. (ed.), Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, Cambridge 1857 (scan vol. 1: archive.org sanctiirenaeiep01harvgoog), read from archive.org djvu OCR (https://archive.org/details/sanctiirenaeiep01harvgoog); ligatures normalised (ae/oe). OCR prints 'precellere' for 'praecellere'. Not visually checked (p.350). No Greek survives for this sentence.
english: For it is fitting that He should excel all [in knowledge]. For how stands the case, for instance, if we endeavour to explain the cause of the rising of the Nile? (ANF 2.28.2)
page: printed p.350 (Harvey vol. 1); ANF page unknown
edition: Harvey 1857 (Cambridge), scan vol. 1; ANF vol. 1 (1885) for English
what_it_says: God (the 'eum' of the context) must excel all in knowledge; this is an argument from the limits of human knowledge.
limits: Opponents cite 'excel all' as subordination of a lower God to a higher one. In this passage 'eum' is God in general; it does not say the Son is inferior. OCR only.

greek: Si ergo et in rebus creaturae quaedam quidem eorum adjacent Deo, quaedam autem et in nostram venerunt scientiam, quid mali est, si et eorum quae in Scripturis requiruntur, universis Scripturis spiritalibus existentibus, quaedam quidem absolvimus secundum gratiam Dei, quaedam autem commendamus Deo; et non solum in hoc saeculo, sed et in futuro: ut semper quidem Deus doceat, homo autem semper discat quae sunt a Deo?
greek_edition: Latin: Harvey, W. W. (ed.), Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, Cambridge 1857 (scan vol. 1: archive.org sanctiirenaeiep01harvgoog), read from archive.org djvu OCR (https://archive.org/details/sanctiirenaeiep01harvgoog); ligatures normalised (ae/oe). Read on the scan at PDF p.575 (= printed p.351), visually confirmed. The Greek of this section is in the next item.
english: If, therefore, even with respect to creation, there are some things [the knowledge of] which belongs only to God, and others which come within the range of our own knowledge, what ground is there for complaint, if, in regard to those things which we investigate in the Scriptures (which are throughout spiritual), we are able by the grace of God to explain some of them, while we must leave others in the hands of God, ... so that God should for ever teach, and man should for ever learn the things taught him by God? (ANF 2.28.3)
page: printed p.351 (Harvey vol. 1); ANF page unknown
edition: Harvey 1857 (Cambridge), scan vol. 1; ANF vol. 1 (1885) for English
what_it_says: Some things about creation and Scripture are known only to God; God always teaches and man always learns.
limits: Says nothing explicit about the Son. 'commendamus Deo' (leave to God) renders a Greek verb whose reading is disputed (see next item). Harvey's English footnote 4 is editorial.

ref: 2.28.3 (Greek preserved in John of Damascus, as printed by Harvey); Harvey p.351 n.2
greek: Εἰ καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν τῆς κτίσεως ἕνια μὲν ἀνάκειται τῷ Θεῷ, ἕνια δὲ καὶ εἰς γνῶσιν ἐλήλυθε τὴν ἡμετέραν, τί χαλεπόν, εἰ καὶ τῶν ἐν ταῖς γραφαῖς ζητουμένων, ὅλων τῶν γραφῶν πνευματικῶν οὐσῶν, ἕνια μὲν ἐπιλύομεν κατὰ χάριν Θεοῦ, ἕνια δὲ ἀνακείσεται τῷ Θεῷ, καὶ οὐ μόνον αἰῶνι ἐν τῷ νυνὶ, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐν τῷ μέλλοντι· ἵνα ἀεὶ μὲν ὁ Θεὸς διδάσκῃ, ἄνθρωπος δὲ διὰ παντὸς μανθάνῃ παρὰ Θεοῦ;
greek_edition: Greek (surviving): Harvey 1857 p.351 (PDF p.575), marginal refs 'Joh. Damasc. Parall.' and 'Halloix'; read on the scan image and matched to the Migne PG 7 Greek OCR (archive.org patrologiae_cursus_completus_gr_vol_007_irenaeus_tomus_unicus). Harvey's footnote 2 says the Latin 'commendamus' suggests the translator read ἀναθήσομεν, and gives GR. variant ἀνατιθέμεθα; the printed Greek verb is ἀνακείσεται. Accents as printed.
english: If, therefore, even with respect to creation, there are some things [the knowledge of] which belongs only to God, and others which come within the range of our own knowledge, what ground is there for complaint, if, in regard to those things which we investigate in the Scriptures ... we are able by the grace of God to explain some of them, while we must leave others in the hands of God ... (ANF 2.28.3; same passage as item I2-04).
page: printed p.351 (Harvey vol. 1); ANF page unknown
edition: Harvey 1857 (Cambridge), scan vol. 1; ANF vol. 1 (1885) for English
what_it_says: Greek of Haer. 2.28.3: some things belong to God, some are known to us; God ever teaches, man ever learns.
limits: Greek survives only through John of Damascus as quoted by Harvey; I did not open the Damascene text itself. Reading 'ἀνακείσεται' (Harvey footnote 2 says Latin implies a different verb). No Greek for 'dispositio' or 'prolatio' here.

greek: Cogitate enim, o omnes qui talia adinvenitis, cum ipse solus Pater Deus dicatur, qui et vere est, quem vos Demiurgum dicitis; sed et cum Scripturae hunc solum sciunt Deum; sed et cum Dominus hunc solum confitetur proprium Patrem, et alterum nesciat, sicut ex ipsis ejus verbis ostendemus:
greek_edition: Latin: Harvey, W. W. (ed.), Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, Cambridge 1857 (scan vol. 1: archive.org sanctiirenaeiep01harvgoog), read from archive.org djvu OCR (https://archive.org/details/sanctiirenaeiep01harvgoog); ligatures normalised (ae/oe). Read on the scan at PDF p.577 (= printed p.353), visually confirmed. Harvey's footnote 6 gives a Greek retroversion 'ὑστερήματος καρπὸν καὶ ἀγνοίας προβολὴν ἀποφαίνεσθε' marked 'BILL.' (scan); this is not surviving Irenaeus Greek. Footnote 4: GRABE reads 'qui sit'.
english: For consider, all you who invent such opinions, since the Father Himself is alone called God, who has a real existence, but whom you style the Demiurge; since, moreover, the Scriptures acknowledge Him alone as God; and yet again, since the Lord confesses Him alone as His own Father, and knows no other, as I shall show from His very words ... (ANF 2.28.4, Roberts & Rambaut).
page: printed p.353 (Harvey vol. 1); ANF page unknown
edition: Harvey 1857 (Cambridge), scan vol. 1; ANF vol. 1 (1885) for English
what_it_says: Gnostics call the Father alone God and the Demiurge a fruit of defect; Irenaeus answers that the Father alone is God and the Lord confesses no other Father.
limits: Unitarian and Arian use: 'the Father alone is God' and 'the Lord knows no other Father'. Irenaeus's target here is the Demiurge, not the Son; he does not in this sentence say how the Son is God. Greek 'ὑστερήματος' is a retroversion only.

greek: Deus autem totus exsistens Mens, et totus exsistens Logos, quod cogitat, hoc et loquitur; quod loquitur, hoc et cogitat. Cogitatio enim ejus Logos, et Logos Mens, et omnia concludens Mens, ipse est Pater.
greek_edition: Latin: Harvey, W. W. (ed.), Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, Cambridge 1857 (scan vol. 1: archive.org sanctiirenaeiep01harvgoog), read from archive.org djvu OCR (https://archive.org/details/sanctiirenaeiep01harvgoog); ligatures normalised (ae/oe). The second sentence ('quod loquitur ... ipse est Pater') read on the scan, PDF p.579 (printed p.355). The first sentence is OCR only (printed p.354). Harvey's chapter heading (Grabe's summary: 'Nus Logos, et Logos Nus, et Nus ipse est Pater omnium') is an editorial heading, not Irenaeus's text.
english: But God being all Mind, and all Logos, both speaks exactly what He thinks, and thinks exactly what He speaks. For His thought is Logos, and Logos is Mind, and Mind comprehending all things is the Father Himself. (ANF 2.28.5, Roberts & Rambaut)
page: printed pp.354-355 (Harvey vol. 1); ANF page unknown
edition: Harvey 1857 (Cambridge), scan vol. 1; ANF vol. 1 (1885) for English
what_it_says: God is all Mind and all Logos; the Logos is God's thought and the all-comprehending Mind is the Father himself.
limits: The text identifies Logos with Mind and says Mind is the Father: a hard sentence for a Trinitarian reader (modalist-sounding). It sits in an anti-Valentinian argument; it does not distinguish persons. Scholarly defences were not consulted in this assignment.

greek: Qui ergo dicit mentem Dei, et prolationem propriam menti donat, compositum eum pronuntiat, tanquam aliud quiddam sit Deus, aliud autem principalis Mens existens. Similiter autem rursus et de Logo, tertiam prolationem ei a Patre donans: unde et ignorat magnitudinem ejus; porro et longe Logon a Deo separavit.
greek_edition: Latin: Harvey, W. W. (ed.), Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, Cambridge 1857 (scan vol. 1: archive.org sanctiirenaeiep01harvgoog), read from archive.org djvu OCR (https://archive.org/details/sanctiirenaeiep01harvgoog); ligatures normalised (ae/oe). Read on the scan, PDF p.579 (printed p.355), visually confirmed. Harvey's margin: 'MASS. II. xxviii. 5'.
english: So, again, with respect to Logos, when one attributes to him the third place of production from the Father; on which supposition he is ignorant of His greatness; and thus Logos has been far separated from God. (ANF 2.28.5, Roberts & Rambaut; the preceding sentence on the 'mind' is in the same paragraph.)
page: printed p.355 (Harvey vol. 1); ANF page unknown
edition: Harvey 1857 (Cambridge), scan vol. 1; ANF vol. 1 (1885) for English
what_it_says: Irenaeus rejects making the Logos a third emission (prolatio) from the Father and says separating the Logos from God is an error.
limits: Shows that Irenaeus rejects an emanationist model of the Logos, but not that he uses 'generation' of the Son here; the word 'prolatio' is used by him in the Gnostic sense in the same passage. No surviving Greek for 'prolatio' here.

greek: Irrationabiliter autem inflati, audaciter inenarrabilia Dei mysteria scire vos dicitis; quandoquidem et Dominus, ipse Filius Dei, ipsum judicii diem et horam concessit scire solum Patrem, manifeste dicens: De die autem illa, et hora nemo scit, neque Filius, nisi Pater solus.
greek_edition: Latin: Harvey, W. W. (ed.), Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, Cambridge 1857 (scan vol. 1: archive.org sanctiirenaeiep01harvgoog), read from archive.org djvu OCR (https://archive.org/details/sanctiirenaeiep01harvgoog); ligatures normalised (ae/oe). Read on the scan, PDF p.579 (printed p.355), visually confirmed. Margin 'Marc. xiii. 32'. Harvey footnote 2: the words 'neque angeli in coelo' (Mark 13:32) are absent from every known text and version; Irenaeus quotes from memory.
english: But, beyond reason inflated [with your own wisdom], you presumptuously maintain that you are acquainted with the unspeakable mysteries of God; while even the Lord, the very Son of God, allowed that the Father alone knows the very day and hour of judgment, when He plainly declares, But of that day and that hour knows no man, neither the Son, but the Father only. (ANF 2.28.6, Roberts & Rambaut)
page: printed p.355 (Harvey vol. 1); ANF page unknown
edition: Harvey 1857 (Cambridge), scan vol. 1; ANF vol. 1 (1885) for English
what_it_says: Irenaeus quotes Mark 13:32 in Latin, with 'neque Filius, nisi Pater solus' (neither the Son but the Father alone).
limits: This is the core Arian/unitarian text: the Son is said not to know the day. The Latin omits 'neque angeli in coelo'. The Greek NT text of Mark 13:32 was not checked here; the Latin is quoted as printed.

greek: Si igitur scientiam diei illius Filius non erubuit referre ad Patrem, sed dixit quod verum est, neque nos erubescamus, quae sunt in quaestionibus majora secundum nos, reservare Deo. Nemo enim super magistrum est.
greek_edition: Latin: Harvey, W. W. (ed.), Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, Cambridge 1857 (scan vol. 1: archive.org sanctiirenaeiep01harvgoog), read from archive.org djvu OCR (https://archive.org/details/sanctiirenaeiep01harvgoog); ligatures normalised (ae/oe). Read on the scan, PDF p.579 (printed p.355), visually confirmed. ANF's own cross-reference for 'no man is superior to his master' is Matthew 10:24; Luke 11:40 (Harvey's margin for this page not checked).
english: If, then, the Son was not ashamed to ascribe the knowledge of that day to the Father only, but declared what was true regarding the matter, neither let us be ashamed to reserve for God those greater questions which may occur to us. For no man is superior to his master. (ANF 2.28.6, Roberts & Rambaut)
page: printed p.355 (Harvey vol. 1); ANF page unknown
edition: Harvey 1857 (Cambridge), scan vol. 1; ANF vol. 1 (1885) for English
what_it_says: Irenaeus's answer to Mark 13:32: the Son referred the knowledge of the day to the Father, as a servant defers to his master.
limits: The master/servant analogy is open to a subordinationist reading; the answer does not say the Son is not God. This is the point where Nicene defenders and Arians part company; no scholarly defence was read for this item.

greek: Si quis itaque nobis dixerit: Quomodo ergo Filius prolatus a Patre est? dicimus ei, quia prolationem istam, sive generationem, sive nuncupationem, sive adapertionem, aut quolibet quis nomine vocaverit generationem ejus inenarrabilem existentem, nemo novit; non Valentinus, non Marcion, neque Saturninus, neque Basilides, neque angeli, neque archangeli, neque principatus, neque potestates, nisi solus qui generavit Pater, et qui natus est Filius.
greek_edition: Latin: Harvey, W. W. (ed.), Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, Cambridge 1857 (scan vol. 1: archive.org sanctiirenaeiep01harvgoog), read from archive.org djvu OCR (https://archive.org/details/sanctiirenaeiep01harvgoog); ligatures normalised (ae/oe). Read on the scan, PDF p.579 (printed p.355), visually confirmed. Harvey footnote 3 gives Greek 'κλῆσιν ἢ ἀνακάλυψιν' for 'nuncupationem, sive adapertionem' (no attribution visible): a retroversion, not Irenaeus's Greek. Footnote 1: 'i.e. a Patre; Bythus, Nous, Logos'.
english: If any one, therefore, says to us, How then was the Son produced by the Father? we reply to him, that no man understands that production, or generation, or calling, or revelation, or by whatever name one may describe His generation, which is in fact altogether indescribable. Neither Valentinus, nor Marcion, nor Saturninus, nor Basilides, nor angels, nor archangels, nor principalities, nor powers [possess this knowledge], but the Father only who begot, and the Son who was begotten. (ANF 2.28.6, Roberts & Rambaut)
page: printed p.355 (Harvey vol. 1); ANF page unknown
edition: Harvey 1857 (Cambridge), scan vol. 1; ANF vol. 1 (1885) for English
what_it_says: The mode of the Son's origin ('prolatio', 'generatio', 'nuncupatio', 'adapertio') is unknowable; only the Father who begets and the Son who is begotten know it.
limits: Irenaeus uses 'prolatio' and 'generatio' as synonyms here, in the Gnostic vocabulary. The answer is about the mode, not the fact, of generation. Greek 'prolatio' behind this sentence does not survive. The Latin 'Filius prolatus' in the question is the objector's phrasing.

greek: Quoniam enim ex cogitatione et sensu verbum emittitur, hoc utique omnes sciunt homines. Non ergo magnum quid invenerunt, qui emissiones excogitaverunt, neque absconditum mysterium, si id quod ab omnibus intelligitur, transtulerunt in unigenitum Dei Verbum: et quem inenarrabilem et innominabilem vocant, hunc, quasi ipsi obstetricaverint, primae generationis ejus prolationem et generationem enuntiant, assimilantes eum hominum verbo emissionis.
greek_edition: Latin: Harvey, W. W. (ed.), Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, Cambridge 1857 (scan vol. 1: archive.org sanctiirenaeiep01harvgoog), read from archive.org djvu OCR (https://archive.org/details/sanctiirenaeiep01harvgoog); ligatures normalised (ae/oe). Read on the scan, PDF p.579 (printed p.355), up to 'prolationem et generationem'; the closing words 'enuntiant, assimilantes eum hominum verbo emissionis' are OCR only (printed p.356, PDF p.580, not visually checked). Harvey footnote 7 is a stray note marker in the OCR ('7. homines').
english: For that a word is uttered at the bidding of thought and mind, all men indeed well understand. Those, therefore, who have excogitated [the theory of] emissions have not discovered anything great, or revealed any abstruse mystery, when they have simply transferred what all understand to the only-begotten Word of God; and while they style Him unspeakable and unnameable, they nevertheless set forth the production and formation of His first generation, as if they themselves had assisted at His birth, thus assimilating Him to the word of mankind formed by emissions. (ANF 2.28.6, Roberts & Rambaut)
page: printed pp.355-356 (Harvey vol. 1); ANF page unknown
edition: Harvey 1857 (Cambridge), scan vol. 1; ANF vol. 1 (1885) for English
what_it_says: Irenaeus rejects the Gnostic 'emission' theory of the Word and calls the Son the only-begotten Word of God.
limits: Only the 'unigenitum Dei Verbum' phrase and the critique of emissions support the reading; the human-word analogy used here is Irenaeus's own. The closing words are OCR only.

greek: Etenim si quis exquirat causam, propter quam in omnibus Pater communicans Filio, solus scire horam et diem a Domino manifestatus est, neque aptabilem magis, neque decentiorem, nec sine periculo alteram quam hanc inveniat in praesenti, quoniam enim solus verax magister est Dominus, ut discamus per ipsum super omnia esse Patrem. Etenim Pater, ait, major me est.
greek_edition: Latin: Harvey, W. W. (ed.), Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, Cambridge 1857 (scan vol. 1: archive.org sanctiirenaeiep01harvgoog), read from archive.org djvu OCR (https://archive.org/details/sanctiirenaeiep01harvgoog); ligatures normalised (ae/oe). Read on the scan, PDF p.581 (printed p.357), visually confirmed. Margin: 'Joh. xiv. 28'. Harvey footnote 5: the Clermont MS. omits 'Pater' before 'major me est'; footnote 4: 'quoniam' = ὅτι γάρ (GRABE).
english: For if any one should inquire the reason why the Father, who has fellowship with the Son in all things, has been declared by the Lord alone to know the hour and the day [of judgment], he will find at present no more suitable, or becoming, or safe reason than this (since, indeed, the Lord is the only true Master), that we may learn through Him that the Father is above all things. For the Father, says He, is greater than I. John 14:28 (ANF 2.28.8, Roberts & Rambaut)
page: printed p.357 (Harvey vol. 1); ANF page unknown
edition: Harvey 1857 (Cambridge), scan vol. 1; ANF vol. 1 (1885) for English
what_it_says: The Father alone is declared to know the hour; this teaches that the Father is above all things, and the Lord cites John 14:28 'the Father is greater than I'.
limits: Subordinationist text: 'super omnia esse Patrem' and 'Pater major me est'. The Latin shows 'Pater communicans Filio' (the Father shares all things with the Son), which the defence would need to set against it. Harvey notes 'Pater' is omitted in one MS. No scholarly defence consulted.

ref: 2.30.9 (ANF); Harvey CAP. XLVII (printed p.368; Massuet 2.30.9 per margin)
greek: Sed solus unus Deus fabricator, hic qui est super omnem principalitatem, et potestatem, et dominationem, et virtutem: hic Pater, hic Deus, hic conditor, hic factor, hic fabricator, qui fecit ea per semetipsum, hoc est per Verbum et per Sapientiam suam, coelum et terram, et maria, et omnia quae in eis sunt:
greek_edition: Latin: Harvey, W. W. (ed.), Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, Cambridge 1857 (scan vol. 1: archive.org sanctiirenaeiep01harvgoog), read from archive.org djvu OCR (https://archive.org/details/sanctiirenaeiep01harvgoog); ligatures normalised (ae/oe). Read on the scan, PDF p.592 (printed p.368), visually confirmed. Harvey footnote 4: 'Verbum et Sapientiam, the synonyms in IV. xxxvii. of Filius et Spiritus' (editorial cross-reference, not Irenaeus). Margin 'Heb. i. 3' for 'Verbo virtutis suae'. No Greek survives.
english: ...He is the Former, He the Builder, He the Discoverer, He the Creator, He the Lord of all ... He it is who ... made those things by Himself, that is, through His Word and His Wisdom — heaven and earth, and the seas, and all things that are in them ... (ANF 2.30.9, Roberts & Rambaut, abridged).
page: printed p.368 (Harvey vol. 1); ANF page unknown
edition: Harvey 1857 (Cambridge), scan vol. 1; ANF vol. 1 (1885) for English
what_it_says: The one God made all things through his own Word and Wisdom, against the Demiurge of the Gnostics.
limits: The Latin says 'Verbum et Sapientiam'; it does not say 'Word and Spirit', and the phrase 'always with Him' from the brief is not in 2.30.9. The identification Wisdom = Spirit is Harvey's cross-reference (IV.xxxvii) and needs Book 4 checked, which was outside this assignment.

greek: Hic Pater Domini nostri Jesu Christi, per Verbum suum, qui est Filius ejus, per eum revelatur et manifestatur omnibus, quibus revelatur: cognoscunt enim eum hi, quibus revelaverit Filius. Semper autem coexsistens Filius Patri, olim et ab initio semper revelat Patrem, et Angelis, et Archangelis, et Potestatibus, et Virtutibus, et omnibus, quibus vult revelare [f. l. revelari] Deus.
greek_edition: Latin: Harvey, W. W. (ed.), Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, Cambridge 1857 (scan vol. 1: archive.org sanctiirenaeiep01harvgoog), read from archive.org djvu OCR (https://archive.org/details/sanctiirenaeiep01harvgoog); ligatures normalised (ae/oe). Read on the scan, PDF p.592 (printed p.368), visually confirmed. '[f. l. revelari]' is Harvey's variant note inside the Latin.
english: He is the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ: through His Word, who is His Son, through Him He is revealed and manifested to all to whom He is revealed; for those [only] know Him to whom the Son has revealed Him. But the Son, eternally co-existing with the Father, from of old, yea, from the beginning, always reveals the Father to Angels, Archangels, Powers, Virtues, and all to whom He wills that God should be revealed. (ANF 2.30.9, Roberts & Rambaut)
page: printed p.368 (Harvey vol. 1); ANF page unknown
edition: Harvey 1857 (Cambridge), scan vol. 1; ANF vol. 1 (1885) for English
what_it_says: The Son is the Word who is co-existing with the Father from the beginning and always reveals the Father.
limits: The Latin 'semper coexsistens ... ab initio' supports eternal co-existence, but the text does not use 'consubstantial' or define the mode of co-existence. The Greek behind 'coexsistens' does not survive here.

ref: 2.35.3 (ANF); Harvey CAP. LVIII sec. 1 (printed p.387; Massuet 2.35.3)
greek: Omnia unius ejusdemque nuncupationis sunt: sicut (secundum Latinitatem) Dominus virtutum, et Pater omnium, et Deus omnipotens, et Altissimus, et Dominus coelorum, et Creator, et Fabricator, et similia his, non alterius atque alterius haec sunt, sed unius ejusdemque nuncupationes et pronomina, per quae unus Deus et Pater ostenditur, qui continet omnia, et omnibus ut sint praestans.
greek_edition: Latin: Harvey, W. W. (ed.), Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, Cambridge 1857 (scan vol. 1: archive.org sanctiirenaeiep01harvgoog), read from archive.org djvu OCR (https://archive.org/details/sanctiirenaeiep01harvgoog); ligatures normalised (ae/oe). Read on the scan, PDF p.611 (printed p.387), visually confirmed. Harvey footnote 1: the bracketed '(secundum Latinitatem)' is the translator's insertion, because he altered Greek divine names into Latin synonyms. The Hebrew-name paragraph before it (Eloe, Eloeim, Adonai, Sabaoth, Jaoth; printed pp.384-386) is OCR only and garbled in places ('Elos verum' / 'Elow', footnote 4 'Elōeim').
english: All the other expressions likewise bring out the title of one and the same Being; as, for example, The Lord of Powers, The Father of all, God Almighty, The Most High, The Creator, The Maker, and such like. These are not the names and titles of a succession of different beings, but of one and the same, by means of which the one God and Father is revealed, He who contains all things ... (ANF 2.35.3, Roberts & Rambaut).
page: printed p.387 (Harvey vol. 1); ANF page unknown
edition: Harvey 1857 (Cambridge), scan vol. 1; ANF vol. 1 (1885) for English
what_it_says: Hebrew and other divine names all refer to one and the same God and Father, who contains all things.
limits: Answers the objection that the Hebrew names show different gods (Gnostic). Says nothing about the Son or Spirit. The Latin names are Harvey's/the translator's Latinised forms.

ref: 2.35.4 (ANF); Harvey CAP. LVIII sec. 2 (printed p.387; Massuet 2.35.4)
greek: Quoniam autem dictis nostris consonat praedicatio Apostolorum, et Domini magisterium, et Prophetarum annuntiatio, et Apostolorum dictatio, et legislationis ministratio, unum eundemque omnium Deum Patrem laudantium; et non alium atque alium, neque ex diversis diis aut virtutibus substantiam habentem; sed ex uno et eodem Patre omnia, (qui tamen aptat secundum subjacentium naturas et dispositionem) et neque ab Angelis, neque ab alia quadam virtute, sed a solo Deo Patre visibilia atque invisibilia, et omnia omnino quaecunque facta sunt,
greek_edition: Latin: Harvey, W. W. (ed.), Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, Cambridge 1857 (scan vol. 1: archive.org sanctiirenaeiep01harvgoog), read from archive.org djvu OCR (https://archive.org/details/sanctiirenaeiep01harvgoog); ligatures normalised (ae/oe). Read on the scan, PDF p.611 (printed p.387), visually confirmed. Harvey footnote 3 gives Greek 'τῶν ὑποκειμένων φύσεις καὶ διαθέσεως' (GRABE, retroversion) for 'subjacentium naturas et dispositionem'; no surviving Greek for 'dispositio' here. Footnote 2 marks 'legislationis'.
english: ...all of which praise one and the same Being, the God and Father of all, and not many diverse beings, nor one deriving his substance from different gods or powers, but [declare] that all things [were formed] by one and the same Father ... things visible and invisible ... neither by angels, nor by any other power, but by God alone, the Father ... (ANF 2.35.4, Roberts & Rambaut, abridged).
page: printed p.387 (Harvey vol. 1); ANF page unknown
edition: Harvey 1857 (Cambridge), scan vol. 1; ANF vol. 1 (1885) for English
what_it_says: All the apostolic and prophetic teaching names one God and Father, by whom all things, visible and invisible, were made, 'by God alone, the Father', not by angels or any other power.
limits: Strongest sentence against an agency of the Son in creation: 'a solo Deo Patre'. It is contrasted with angels and powers, and sits beside 2.30.9 (through the Word and Wisdom). A Trinitarian reader must read 'solo Deo Patre' as excluding creatures, not the Word. No defence consulted.
